reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard haematology references
clinicalPearls: A group of rare inherited anaemias defined by ineffective erythropoiesis and characteristic morphological abnormalities of erythroblasts in the bone marrow
The anaemia is typically accompanied by an inappropriately low reticulocyte count, indirect hyperbilirubinaemia and jaundice, mimicking a haemolytic picture
Three classic types are recognised, distinguished by marrow morphology and genetics: type I (CDAN1/CDIN1), type II (SEC23B, the most common), and the rarer type III
Type II, historically known as HEMPAS, shows binucleate and multinucleate erythroblasts and a positive acidified serum lysis test with some sera
Iron overload develops from ineffective erythropoiesis with increased iron absorption, even in patients who are not regularly transfused
Splenomegaly is common and splenectomy can raise haemoglobin in some patients, though it does not correct the underlying defect
Management principles are supportive: monitoring and treating iron overload with chelation, transfusion when required, folate support, and consideration of splenectomy in selected cases
It is frequently misdiagnosed as a haemolytic anaemia or thalassaemia, so marrow morphology and genetic testing are key to the diagnosis
Allogeneic stem cell transplantation is reserved for severe transfusion-dependent disease
reference.pathophysiology: The congenital dyserythropoietic anaemias are caused by inherited mutations affecting erythroid maturation, differing by subtype (for example CDAN1 or CDIN1 in type I and SEC23B in type II). The common mechanism is ineffective erythropoiesis: erythroid precursors proliferate in the marrow but undergo abnormal maturation and intramedullary death, so relatively few mature red cells reach the circulation despite marrow hyperplasia. The resulting anaemia with low reticulocyte response is accompanied by increased iron absorption driven by ineffective erythropoiesis, leading to progressive iron overload independent of transfusion. Characteristic morphological abnormalities of erythroblasts (multinuclearity, internuclear bridging, abnormal chromatin) are diagnostic clues specific to each type.
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and reticulocyte count showing anaemia with inappropriately low reticulocytes
Bone marrow examination for characteristic dyserythropoietic morphology and, in type II, electron microscopy
Serum bilirubin, LDH and haptoglobin to characterise the ineffective/haemolytic picture
Iron studies and organ iron assessment for overload
Molecular genetic testing to subclassify (CDAN1/CDIN1, SEC23B and others)
redFlags: Complications of iron overload affecting the heart, liver or endocrine organs
Features suggesting evolution to a myelodysplastic process
Aplastic crisis in the context of parvovirus B19 infection
reference.prognosis: Most patients have chronic anaemia of variable severity compatible with long survival, but the dominant long-term threat is iron overload, which can cause serious cardiac, hepatic and endocrine complications if not monitored and chelated. Outlook is generally good with attentive management of iron burden and anaemia.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the disorder as a haemolytic anaemia or thalassaemia and missing the diagnosis
Failing to monitor and chelate iron in non-transfused patients who still accumulate iron
Assuming splenectomy corrects the underlying defect
Overlooking the need for genetic subtyping to guide counselling
Not recognising aplastic crises triggered by parvovirus B19
